=== FILE: 20 minutes for better pushups [0vhfofRr_qs].en.txt ===

Here's a 20-minute routine to help you get better at push-ups. Okay, first just move around a bit to warm up. Then do one set of an easier variation where you only do about half as many reps as you think you can. Then you can rest for about a minute and then you can start the foundation of the workout where you do three sets of the hardest variation you can safely do for at least five clean solid reps. Rest long enough between sets for you to go ham on the next set. Do as many reps as you safely can, but when your last rep kind of looks like this, you can probably end the set. And this isn't for everybody, but if you're still working on getting your first clean full range of motion push-up, some people find success from practicing the top part of the movement that they can do as long as it's slow, controlled, and painfree. But wait, what about full range of motion? Well, afterwards, you can follow up with a few sets of an easier variation that you can control through a full range of motion. This way, you can start to learn the feeling of a full push-up while you train yourself through a full range of motion that you can do with good technique. And finally, you can finish with an isometric set where you either hold at the bottom if you can do that or just push about 50 70% and try to press up if you can't yet do that. This can help your body and especially your joints get used to the bottom part of movement which is usually the hardest. Have a beautiful day.

=== FILE: 200 chicken nuggets [HcPS_9pSnIg].en.txt ===

10,000 calories is like 200 chicken nuggets. And the reason that's important is because some people start working out and they immediately start gaining some weight the next day, which for me would be like, woo, because I usually have to focus to gain some weight. But if your goal is to lose weight, I can see how that'd be a bit of a bummer because you get all motivated and the next day you get what seems to be negative feedback. Which is why I think it's important to know that it's actually quite unlikely for you to gain several pounds of fat in a single day. It's actually quite difficult. Three l pounds of fat would be like 10,000 calories, which is a lot of chicken nuggies. And where that weight might actually come from is some slight inflammation from your body trying to recover from your workout, which is good and normal. And it might be your body putting some extra energy stores in your muscles because you're getting strong. So, what you can do instead is you don't have to track with a scale if you don't want. There are some other ways to track progress. And if you want to track with a scale, then you can measure every few days around the same time and conditions and chart your progress and see where the direction is going because everyone fluctuates a bit dayto-day.

=== FILE: 3 Common Beginner Fitness Mistakes [XbAXhiNq0jQ].en.txt ===

hey friends here are three common fitness mistakes that beginners make the first is trying to spot reduce fat with exercise it's well known that we can grow our muscles by doing exercises that train that area so it might seem intuitive to think that if we want to lose fat in any given area then we should also work that area unfortunately this is not known to be possible with diet and exercise we lose fat throughout the body if you want to lose fat anywhere i personally recommend muscle building exercises larger muscles increase the energy demands of our body the second mistake is thinking that you have to exercise every day we often try to make up years of inactivity by doing a lot of exercise very quickly this can lead to burnout and then months will go by before you start working out again instead you might want to try working out two to three times a week and increase volume as you become more consistent don't worry about having a perfect and balanced routine right away the third mistake is thinking you need a bunch of expensive gear look i own an online fitness store i sell fitness products i use them they're handy but all you really need to get started is the floor and gravity last i checked those were free don't let other people sell you junk you don't need even if it's me bernard what do you say well said

=== FILE: Build a Strong Core Without Endless Reps [XsoE0etubnY].txt ===

 Core strength is very important to develop in fitness, but unfortunately, there are a few key misunderstandings that hold some people back, so I want to share three key points that I think will really help you once you understand. And the good news is that after you understand them, then core strength will just pretty much never be an issue for you again. And then you can just go on to do a lot of cool stuff and, you know, just be awesome. And the last point is something I learned in my first year of fitness, but it's not really something I hear discussed that much. The first is that we tend to train our core as if it were just our abs, when there's quite a bit more to it than that, and yet a lot of us still default to front-facing things, like leg raises and ups and even crunches, because it can help us feel the burn here. And this breaks down into two separate but related issues, and the first is actually good news, which is our core is designed to work together. So whatever core exercise you're doing is probably still training your core, and it's very important for it to stabilize so we can move like this and still stay rigid as needed. And we want our core to be strong enough to protect us and stabilize us through a variety of different movement, whether we are lifting ourselves or lifting something else. And this means that we don't usually have to isolate our core training unless we're trying to body build or have a very specific need. And your core has the potential to be very strong. It's designed to be very strong because it needs to maintain an up-tension to protect and support one of the most important parts of our bodies, which is our biceps, of course, right? Very important. No, our spine, right? It's essential to many parts of life, and that's why our core is designed to protect it. So we core, no fun, but a strong core not only can make you better at athletic movement and exercise, but can also help protect your life and quality of living. By the way, that bicep kiss, I once did that in public accidentally. I had this thing where I lean over to my wife sometimes when we're eating in a restaurant and I'll kiss her and I lean over and I didn't realize that she had a long sleeve on. So I just kissed the only bare skin that I saw, which was my own bicep. So I was like, I love you. And she was like, did you just kiss your own bicep? In my mind, I didn't register that it was weird. I was like, yeah, but like in my mind, it was actually yours, but I didn't want to kiss your sleeves. So I just kissed, nevermind. And the second issue is that a lot of us are chasing the burn when we're doing core exercises, when that's not really what will advance us. I don't know if you could see me, but I decided I wanted to do some leg raises, but I have this rock here. If I were to ask you about this rock, how many times do you think you could curl this rock? Well, it'd probably be hundreds, right? For some of you, it could be thousands. It's basically just a few pounds, almost no weight, and you could do a lot of it. But you would notice, maybe not even 100 reps in, that you would feel the burn. And that is the potential issue with a lot of core exercises. We pursue things like a plank or sit-ups and crunches, which I am not saying are necessarily bad exercises, especially if that's the level you're at that you need to get stronger to build up. But after you can do hundreds of them, man, if I were to tell you to strengthen any other part of your body and you picked a weight that you could do hundreds of, do you think that would be the best way to get strong? And a lot of people would say, no, not necessarily, yet with our core, we tend to think differently. I know from experience that this can be a small point of contention for some people, because they're like, well, I like doing this, so I don't want to stop doing it. I get it. If you want to do it, and whatever you're doing is working as usual, please keep doing it. What I would say instead is perhaps, if you want to strengthen your core and you think it's an issue, then try some more difficult exercises. They could be leg raises. So if you're working too close to your max ability, you might get closer to the risk of injury, which is not good. But after you can do like, say 20 reps of something, you may want to consider moving on to a slightly harder variation. And the third thing is that while there is a focus on movement in core exercises like sit ups and crunches, one of the most important functions of the core muscles is to resist movement when we pick things up and down, for example. And this breaks up into two slightly smaller points and a bonus at the end. And the first is that you're already doing this, probably if you're training your core, as in you're training your core somewhat with isometrics, even with things like sit ups and leg raises, if you put your hand on your belly, you will feel a little bit of movement, but it's not really that much movement compared to how much your abs are capable of, for example. If you try to touch your sternum to your pubic bone, you realize that, wow, you're suddenly moving a lot more. And even during a sit up, the last part is usually done with hip flexors, for example. === FILE: Deep Lunges are Great for Mobility & Strength [yXVHr7wrleQ].en.txt ===

my friend one of the best things you can do for your strength and mobility is to build up to a nice deep body weight lunge and mobility can really enhance your strength and power unfortunately it's widely accepted in the calisthenics and fitness community that there is no safe way to build up to the lunge if you can't do it just kidding of course there are ways to build up there always are now put your beautiful leg up on a wall and you can do some leg press lunges to acclimate yourself to the movement for all variations try to work both sides equally generally the higher the leg the easier the exercise but eventually you want to work up to something around knee height that allows your hamstrings to entirely cover your calves ideally with your heels completely down and your foot horizontal eventually you can work up to a short lunge like this you can alternate legs if you want or you can just keep walking start stepping further and further until you can do a nice deep body weight lunge now some may wonder if it's safe to have your knees go over your toes well he ain't called knees behind toes guy building up to a full pain-free controlled range of motion is an important part of your fitness journey keeping your back leg as straight as possible can be a nice stretch for your hip flexors having tight hip flexors can cause anterior pelvic tilt which can be a source of lower back pain have a wonderful beautiful day

hello my friend here's how you can build up to an exercise called the elbow lever it's not as hard as it might look and it's a great Core workout you do have an advantage if you get good at push-ups and pull-ups first but as usual you can start with the basics and work your way up work on holding a plank for at least 30 seconds then try it with your feet elevated then experiment with one leg planks both sides of course then work on one arm planks this is very functional if you suddenly have to scratch an itch next hold a plank with your feet pressed against the wall to make it harder you can do it one-legged or just alternate then Jam your elbows into your abs then you can hold an elbow lever against the wall now it gets more interesting spend some time playing with your dog ask her not to pee on the floor find a safe area just work on getting the hole this is probably not the safest area dude from there and there you go congratulations on being a ninja don't be frustrated if you don't get it right away because you are developing strength and balance have a beautiful day

=== FILE: Easy Calisthenics Warmup [RYLw1cMYHX0].en.txt ===

warming up properly can improve the quality of your workouts here's an easy way you can start with some general light aerobic work like jumping jacks or running in place do this for about 60 seconds here you're just trying to loosen up your muscles and warm up your body it doesn't really matter what technique you use i mean your shadow boxing could look like this whatever works next you can just do an easier variation of your workout for example if you're doing full push-ups you can warm up with wall push-ups or incline push-ups do two sets at about 50 of your max and that's really it i like to keep my warm-ups simple you can probably do this in less than five minutes have a beautiful day my friend

=== FILE: Exercise Shouldn't Hurt THIS Much [jsWii7wVBRU].en.txt ===

My friend, exercise should be reducing the amount of pain in your life. If it keeps adding to it, you can try these changes. A good warm-up can be the difference between a workout making you stronger or making you weaker. So, hit some easier variations and literally move to make your body warmer before getting to your main exercises. Even if you're quite strong, move the joints you're about to use and stay out of the range that causes you pain. If it hurts, back off to an easier variation or use some assistance. And two, not everyone needs it, but if you're really stiff, then you can mobilize first. A foam roller or self massage can help your muscles move like they should, but any relaxation work is usually done better after your heavy workouts. And three, you can work your opposing muscles, too. You don't have to be perfectly balanced, but if you do a lot of pushing, then you can try some pulling, too. And this can especially apply to your joints. These small changes can help you feel better and not worse. Have a beautiful day.

 There is a misunderstanding in fitness that I think is actively keeping some people less fit than they could be, and that is, you don't have to work out to be fit, or do you? It depends on how you define working out. Now, working out can be cool and beneficial, and I started a YouTube channel around it, but I do think there is a lazy way to fitness, or a not-enthusiast way to fitness, that a lot of people are already on, and there are some people who want the benefits of working out that they've heard, like living longer, especially as they get older, and having improved quality of life, but they just aren't passionate about working out. So that sounds like you or a friend, then hopefully this can help. But first, I think it's important to understand why we might have this perception of fitness, and do you know how hard it is to get everyone to agree on something? And yet, if you type into a search engine of your choice, exercise is healthy? Enter, then you'll see a lot of people do agree that exercise is healthy, myself included. Sadly, not everyone agrees, but I think a large majority do. So we have that first step, but the next step is what do you think of when you think of exercise? Now, you might think of biking, swimming, maybe sports, but I think a lot of people think about gym stuff, like working out stuff. So like going in, lifting weights, running on treadmills, and even calisthenics stuff like push-ups and pull-ups. So that is fitness, yes, I would say, but is that necessarily fitness and health? If you notice that fitness and health is kind of just like thrown in there, like a fitness center, and it's like, hey, join our center for fitness and health. Sign up today, exercise is good for you. This brings up an interesting question, which is, is fitness and health the same thing? Or perhaps a more visual example is someone who is a paragon of fitness, an ideal of fitness, also a paragon of health? And perhaps not necessarily, right? So we think of someone who's perfectly healthy in your mind, think of someone who's perfectly healthy, and we think of someone who's perfectly fit. And perfectly fit has some associations, again, with exercise and workout culture, right? Which I don't think is bad at all, but you think of someone who is quite athletic looking, muscular, lean, not necessarily the biggest, but you know, quite sporty looking, right? And from here, we can think of that sadly, there are a lot of people who looked like that. And you could say we're very good at their sport and very athletic and perhaps very muscular and strong, who may have unfortunately had some health side effects or maybe even died early because they trained and may have put some things in their body in pursuit of that fitness and ability that might have ended up making them less healthy. So I would say no, they're not quite the same thing. It makes sense. They're connected. They're deservedly so, I would say, but they're not quite the same thing. Fitness and health as a Venn diagram is not quite a circle. There's just some lumps on the side. But of course, there is research and of course, there are very intelligent, well read people talking about how exercise is good for you. And Hampton, didn't you show all those things? What I'm trying to say is that there are some pursuits that are separate that we might have conflated. We might have connected in our mind. So we think about someone who is using physical activity for the purpose of being healthy and someone exercising for the purpose of getting stronger or looking very muscular and someone training for the purpose of being very good at their sport. I would say these are related, but they're slightly separate. And what this leads to is some people think they hear about the benefits of exercise and they say, well, I want to be healthy. I really have no interest in getting that much stronger or being muscular. And I'm not really an athlete. And they think, well, in order for me to be healthy, which is what I've heard, I have to do this stuff and they end up not doing it, which can be an issue. === FILE: I Bear Crawled 1 Mile a Day (for a few months) [mwYi1LTQRzI].en.txt ===

There was a time in my life where I would bear crawl every day as part of my morning workout and I ended up building up to around a mile a day and I'm not really recommending that to anyone but it was interesting. So here are five things I learned from bear crawling a mile a day with the fifth being the most I ever crawled at once and an important lesson that I learned. And the first in the theme of other videos in this series that I've been doing is that I did not really have back pain. I'm actually pretty weak here, so I don't put a lot of force. So, another painfree hold for 30 seconds. And then I'll grab the paralletts again. And this time, we'll work the other side. I don't grab here because it would tilt. So, I grab this side and just try to flex back. I do it at this angle, but you can try different ones. Either way, you're holding for 30, of course. I realized that it was taking more time and energy to get to the place where I felt ready to do the thing than it did to just do the thing. meaning I just try to get in the flow of things as soon as possible because I will feel more focused. === FILE: I set resolutions around habits, not goals [QR1nRV17XuY].en.txt ===

I don't really set New Year's resolutions, but if I did, I wouldn't set them around a goal, but a habit. So, not what do I want to achieve this year, but what are things I can do every day to get me closer to the things that I want. Now, why is it every day? Number one, it's probably not going to be every day. I'll probably have some off days, but I want to aim for often. And number two, it doesn't have to be the same thing every day. So, if it's around fitness, I don't have to work out every day, but I can read and learn and improve my fitness on my rest days. And number three, I want that slight struggle and discomfort as I'm learning this new habit. Because the truth is for me, if the habit already felt great and automatic, I would probably already have it. So, there's a little bit of struggle cost as I learn to install this new behavior. And I try to learn to embrace a process rather than a goal because I have a little bit more control over the process. But if goals motivate you, that is awesome. Have a beautiful day.

=== FILE: I wish I got this before training legs [KaPsAwS5FGE].en.txt ===

If you do any kind of exercise or work where you're on your knees, I highly recommend you get some kind of pad. But there are good and bad ones you can get. And here's how you can tell. Now, if you're doing an exercise where your knee doesn't really move around that much and you're just barely touching the ground like this, or you just need some extra stability and or just aren't moving around a lot, then a solid one can be pretty good. But if you're doing knee push-ups or Nordic curls like I was doing a little while ago, I don't really have a door I can show you around here. then I highly recommend you get some kind of thicker or contoured padding because as I found the constant movement under pressure on my knees was pretty uncomfortable on my kneecap and not in a way that was making it stronger. I am not sure on this, but I think some people have actually dislocated their kneecap this way. So, I got the sticker pad and I do like it a lot better so far. And if I need to, I might cut some holes for my knees to fit in better, but I rather not because smooth. So, I would say consider a solid one if your knees aren't moving on the ground much and you like the stability. But if your knees are hurting, then consider something softer, especially if you're doing some movement on them. I should work on that. Have a beautiful day.

=== FILE: If You Sit All Day, Do This Every Hour [NmfFdlRqQz8].en.txt ===

Instead of trying to undo eight hours of sitting with a bunch of stretches later, we can just take some breaks from the sitting itself. Try setting a timer for every hour or so, and when it goes off, stand up, walk around, maybe shake off a bit, or do some push-ups. This can sometimes be a good way to get your exercise sets in. These small breaks can sometimes work better than the emergency stretches we try to do later after something's wrong. your lack of motivation might not be a bad thing see it's commonly taught in Fitness that waiting for motivation is unreliable that you need discipline to have the consistency to achieve long-term results and while I agree with that why can't we have both if discipline can get you through the race then having motivation and discipline would help you win the race right see I think we're motivated when stuff is working well for us when we start a new exercise routine or a new project but over the months and over the years that motivation can Wane a bit yeah sometimes that can mean we need more discipline and more patience but other times it can mean it's time to try something new see I'm not motivated to go to a public gym some people are and that's awesome for me that lack of motivation wasn't a bug it was a feature it led me to explore working out at home and sharing that with all of you so I would say use discipline to get started and get on the road but use motivation to sometimes explore other roads even if it's just to rule them out have a beautiful day

=== FILE: Lose balance during exercises？ [17hfsmJmNss].en.txt ===

=== FILE: Make any workout more intense (quick tip) [rZRIGOqJBYQ].en.txt ===

=== FILE: New workout leaving you sore？ [RfsEsOrb_0o].en.txt ===

If you just started working out for the first time in a while and you feel very sore, I have good news and bad news. The good news is that you won't always be the sore. As your body gets used to the workouts and you become more fit, you will be less sore after your workout. And the kind of bad news is that soreness isn't necessarily making you any leaner or stronger. So, if you're very sore and it's taking some time to heal, then the sets and reps you do might not be as much as you could do. So, for your first few weeks, you don't have to go 100%. You could go 50 to 70% and increase that as you get used to the exercise. Some gentle movement like walking and getting plenty of rest can also help you heal from your soreness. And bonus, as you get more fit, then you can train more often without being excessively sore. And that can help you make some faster progress. Have a beautiful day.

=== FILE: Pullups Don't Have to Hurt Your Hands [AxBEDP4wosk].en.txt ===

My friend, if doing pull-ups hurts your hands or gives you blisters, that doesn't have to happen. Many people, if they lack grip strength, wrap the bar around their palm and hike up their hands like this. While this isn't necessarily bad, if you're doing this to compensate for lack of grip strength, it may cause blisters. As you lose your grip and your hand starts to slip down, this compresses the skin underneath your knuckles. And that's usually how the blisters or calluses form. See, I like calluses, but I recommend at least learning to wrap the bar around your fingers and not your palm. So, instead of grabbing the bar like this, it would look like this. Try doing a few pull-ups this way to see how it feels. If you can't do pull-ups yet with this new grip, spend a few days a week just learning to hang from the bar. This will make you stronger lickety split. And of course, you can always build up with easier pull-up variations. Just to repeat really quick, don't wrap the palm, wrap the fingers. Things like chalk, cushions, and gloves are useful. I sell these things, but a better long-term investment is to build up your grip strength. Thank you for being your wonderful

Some people tend to do a bunch of easy sets and never really get close to that challenging zone. Others do super heavy sets with only one or two reps or holding for a few seconds. While all of those do have their place, it can be hard to make long-term progress doing only those. The sweet spot is usually a small or moderate number of focused, challenging sets done consistently. Simple rule of thumb. For your big movements like push, pull, and squats, have at least a couple of sets per week where if you had Q, you could only do one to three more reps. === FILE: Stuck on pullups？ [sNsrvDrVVRU].en.txt ===

And if you've done any kind of calisthenics or are familiar with gymnastics at all, then you may have tried something and gotten stuck on an exercise trying to build up to what you want. And just real quick, if you're not familiar with progressions, they're actually one of the best things about calisthenics. So the idea that if you can't do a push-up yet, you can first start up with something like incline push-ups and then you can go down to knee push-ups. But when you try to do full push-ups, you go, you suddenly stall and you were making a lot of progress, which is motivating before, but suddenly you try to do something and you aren't able to do it. I'm going to try something else instead. And to be clear, you can try something else and that's great. But it is sad because this seems to be an issue with not just progressions, but how we approach them. And here's what I mean. So if we think about something like weightlifting, one of the best things about weightlifting is also its progression system. Now we don't usually think of weightlifting as having progressions, but I would argue it actually has hundreds of progressions in the form of small differences in weight. So like pretend these are closer together. But effectively, you start with a weight that you can lift maybe say six times and you practice until you can do it say nine times and then you make the weight a little bit heavier and then maybe back down to six times and you're like, "Okay, cool. === FILE: Tiny Workout Changes, Big Results [JrFypdHlbk8].txt ===

 If I wanted to get dramatically better workout results this year without spending more time at the gym, these are small changes that I would make. Not on your routine, not waking up at 5am before everyone else. It's the few quiet switches that make everything easier and more effective. Hello my friend, it is your brother Hampton from Hybrid Calisthenics. For many people that want to be more fit, they think the answer is more. More time, more effort, more pain, and more can help. But what a lot of us need is more focus. Adding things actually reduces focus. So what actually moved the needle for me and a lot of our community were small changes that slipped into the routine I already had. Today I want to share some of those with you. Think of this as a menu. You don't have to eat everything. Even picking one or two can make a big difference. Let me ask you, if I told you that you can't add more time to your workout, what would you change instead? Your form, your rest, your schedule? Most people never think about this. They only think in terms of adding more. This may work for a few weeks, but most of us don't work out for a living. I guess I kind of do. But even then, eventually we hit a point where we're making progress but can't sustain this long term. That's when some people say I just don't have time to be fit. === FILE: Why I Prefer Pushups To Dips (For Beginners) [RadJF_5Eaqw].en.txt ===

I usually prefer push-ups over dips for beginners only because I found dips to be a bit harder on beginner shoulders. They tend to put your shoulder in a deeper stretch, which can be a good thing, but if you're not used to the movement, can make you quite sore for a few days, which can make it a little bit harder to be consistent starting out. Push-ups usually don't stretch your shoulder as much. Forward pushing can seem a bit more intuitive for some people, and they require slightly less equipment to get started. That said, if you build up properly with easier progressions, both push-ups and dips can be great exercises. And if you adapt to something that used to be hard for you, then you've gotten stronger. Have a beautiful day.

=== FILE: You CAN Do Pushups [L-Yd2YpIDkI].en.txt ===

My friend, if you can't do push-ups, just like with everything else in the world, you can build up. Let me help. There's no reason to be ashamed if you can't do a push-up. Fitness is a journey, and we all start somewhere. Plus, there are many kinds of push-ups. So, we find one we can do, and we work it until we're strong enough to move on. We can start with some wall push-ups. Aim for three sets of 50. The reason you're doing so many is so you can practice your pushing motion. Next, we can do incline push-ups on a railing, table, or any stable surface. The lower the object, the harder. I recommend starting with something at least higher than your hips. Work these until you can do three sets of 40. Next, we finally go back to the ground. And we can do kneeling push-ups. And no, I never call these girl push-ups. This is a great therapy exercise that we don't need to shame. And I've never met a girl that likes them being called that. Anyway, work these until you can do two sets of 25. And then you should be strong enough to do a regular full push-up. Congratulations. If you start getting joint pain, you may have progressed too quickly. Go back to some of the easier variations. Sometimes our muscles are strong enough to move on, but our joints are not. If you're interested, I have a full YouTube video on this that I'll link in the comments. Have a beautiful day.

=== FILE: active hangs VS passive hangs (different benefits) [aGpThXQhHuA].en.txt ===

Dead hangs are popular right now and they offer a variety of cool benefits, but here are some ways you can check to make sure you're doing them right. Now, broadly, there are two types of hangs. You have active and passive. And passive is more of the true dead hang because your muscles are mostly supposed to be relaxed and stretched except for your grip muscles. Your arms should be mostly straight and your shoulders should be up. I kind of have trouble getting them near my ears like they're supposed to be. A lot of people start with passive hangs. So, when you hear about the benefits of hanging, this is usually what people are talking about because you get a nice stretch in your shoulders, upper body, and even midsection. You can improve your grip strength and even strengthen your arms a bit. And an important thing is you're not supposed to feel pain from this. So if you do feel some sharp stabbing joint pain, then you may want to assist a bit with your arms until you get stronger. And I know I'm swinging around on different bars and stuff, but most people start with overhand or around shoulder width apart and build up to around 60 seconds or so. And after you're good at that, you can train some active hangs with your shoulders down and maybe arms slightly engaged. Now, you usually can't hang on quite as long with these and they don't stretch you out quite as much, but they can help you build shoulder stability, which is important for pull-ups and other exercises, and that's always fun. Have a beautiful day.

=== FILE: are electrolyte powders worth it？ [Qni7yJ_hmYc].en.txt ===

People pay a lot of money for these electrolyte powders, so you might wonder if they're worth it. Well, it depends. They usually have some version of sodium, magnesium, potassium, and more. === FILE: how I heal faster (from soreness) [jHl5CMDg9bM].en.txt ===

When I have a muscle that's quite sore, I haven't heard that many people talk about this. But I've learned that I heal faster if I sleep with that area slightly bent. This happens especially so with my calves. The day after I do a full deep range of motion with straight legs, calf raise for a few sets relatively high load. I am just very sore for the next few days. You would think this would come naturally. Thank you. But sleeping with the foot a bit down, the knees a bit bent, it might still feel a bit more stiff in the morning, but not nearly as much. And one of the reasons for this could be because our muscle's resting position is usually with that joint bent and not with it stretched out like you might think. If we were to take the opposite extreme of this and we slept with our joints very stretched, then even though we're not lifting anything, that muscle might still be under tension, which would be passive tension, which can be very useful for lifting and making us stronger. But when we're resting, I kind of want my muscles just to chill out so it can heal and grow. Have a beautiful day.

=== FILE: how to do more reps of anything [jk_fA_19ZiM].en.txt ===

If you want to do more reps of anything, it will really help you to know what's stopping you. There are only like three things it could be. The first is having a weak link that isn't directly part of what you're trying to train. So, if you can do 15 pull-ups without your grip, but your grip only allows you to do five, how many can you do? But if that's your problem, the good news is that you can unlock a lot of growth very quickly because you're basically just showing the strength you already have if you're not limited by your grip strength. So, if you spend some time just hanging after your workout to train your grip strength, or you can just use straps if you want a quick workaround, and that would mean that you can suddenly do like three times as many pull-ups, which is awesome. The second is a mobility or technique issue that's stopping you from working where you're trying to work, which is actually pretty common in something like wall push-ups. People tell me they're stuck at like 25 or something. I'm like, "No, I think you're strong enough to do that." And what I do is I see their wrist way down here, and they are plenty strong enough to do 50 or more wall push-ups, but they're being limited by their wrist strength. They're like, "Ah, it's hurting." So, you're not actually working the pushing muscles you're trying to work. A quick work around for some people is just to use their fingers. By the way, >> there's a weird guy here, so I might just finish up. This can happen across many different exercises. So, next time you're trying to do as many as you can, find out what's stopping you from doing more. If it's something like your knees here, like, oh, I can just adjust how I'm doing this, you can film yourself and watch back and wow, suddenly you can do many more reps. You're amazing. And the last one after you've unlocked those is sometimes you just do need to train or recover a little bit more, which is probably the most boring one. But do a few hard sets maybe twice a week. === FILE: the ＂problem＂ with assisted exercises [_EXOWMwgf78].en.txt ===

Self-assisted exercises are great for helping some people make progress, but a lot of people leave out a key detail. See, the difference between assisting a little bit and assisting a lot doesn't seem like that much, but it can be like 10 or 20 lbs, which is a lot for a single arm exercise. And the reason that's important is you might be getting stronger even if you're doing the same amount of reps. When I first did these, I would leave bruises on my own wrist. And when the bruises stopped and I was doing the same amount of reps, I figured I was assisting less, so I got stronger. But thankfully, there is a better way than that. You can make it more measurable if you use a type of assistance where you aren't able to assist as much even if you're trying as hard as you can. For example, gripping higher can be easier because you can get a better grip. Gripping lower is harder. Similarly, gripping all the way around easier, using flat palm harder. But it's also important to make your assistance specific to the thing you're training because you can use things like fewer fingers and that will feel harder and it will feel tempting to make it more measurable. But in my opinion, this doesn't transfer quite as well to something like the one- arm pull-up. But if it works well for you, that's great. Have a beautiful day.

=== FILE: your ＂half reps＂ aren't necessarily bad [GsOW8ovxwW0].en.txt ===

online fitness culture seems to really enjoy making fun of people who do partial range of motion so much that we forget that it can sometimes be useful when learning new bodyweight skills starting with a range of motion you can handle safely is a valid progression and you can still build strength through a full range of motion by following it up with an easier variation where you can handle that extra range as usual we get better at what we train so if you want to say get a little bit stronger in your top range of motion then you can use a heavier weight than you would otherwise be able to if you went all the way down then you can always add it back as you get stronger you can do half push-ups for example go lower and lower as you get stronger over time really try to feel the muscles working and try to control the movement sure squats to measure depth and use lower chairs as you get stronger even moving your shoulder blades can help you build a stronger foundation for your work play around with it have a beautiful day

=== FILE: ＂good＂ technique is misunderstood (sometimes) [SN3mzHRdjbs].en.txt ===

Good technique doesn't always make you better or stronger. Here's what I mean. There are like three different things people mean when they talk about better technique. The first is an adjustment that'll make the movement stronger or more stable for you. For pull-ups, this can mean learning to unshrug your shoulders and keeping your shoulder blades down to have a more stable movement. It might feel weird if you're not used to it, but you'll probably have more potential that way. And you can improve this with a few focus sets at the end of your workouts. And the second is just being more intentional with your form so you can actually target what you want. And the funny thing is this will sometimes mean you're not lifting as much weight. For example, you could do a straight leg deadlift like this. It's not really like unsafe or anything. You're probably looking more than you could with actually straight legs. It's just not the intention of the exercise that you're actually trying to do. I mean, does this does this leg look straight to you? But then there are also times where it might feel harder at first, but you're working on something that'll make you stronger, like using your chest more during push-ups. Either way, you can improve this by filming your sets and watching back. And third and most important is consistency of form. And this one can make you safer. Injuries sometimes happen when you try a new technique with the same weight as a familiar technique. So, it's okay to try new stuff, but just consider starting lighter. Have a beautiful day.

=== FILE: ＂use what you have＂ pros and cons [CADdWRo5XUA].en.txt ===

One of my favorite things about home workouts is also one of my least favorite things and that is the idea of using what you have. I love the idea that most of us can get fit and strong with just our body and gravity. And I still believe that. But when it comes to something like a pull-up bar, I know that not everyone has access to one, but after like 10 years of trying to get beginners to work with things like tables or elbow presses, I would now start with 10 sets of trying to get a good pull-up bar. You can buy, build, or rent. Now, if what you're doing is working or really all you have, then by all means, please keep doing it. But I have noticed that some beginners may struggle with angles and technique where they're essentially limited by weaker muscles rather than stronger ones. Or they might be frustrated by a lack of progress, but the thing they're trying to use is hard to grip and holding them back. So tree branches and stuff can be great. I have used those, too. But once you're pretty sure that you want to be serious about fitness, then getting some good workout equipment that you can afford might be a worthwhile upgrade. Not financial advice. Have a beautiful day.
